meta.title: Who really said "Etymology is a science in which the vowels count for nothing"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Never found in Voltaire. The idea traces to Antoine Court de Gébelin's Monde primitif (1775); the saying was circulating unattributed by 1833, and only acquired Voltaire's name in the 19th century — decades after his death.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Etymology is a science in which the vowels count for nothing'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Voltaire. Probably originates with Court de Gébelin (1775); the Voltaire credit is a 19th-century attachment, long after he died.

answer.label: Not Voltaire — probably Court de Gébelin
answer.sourceLine: Researchers have never located this in Voltaire’s writings. The nearest ancestor is Antoine Court de Gébelin’s Monde primitif (1775), whose etymological principles include “les voyelles ne sont rien” — vowels count for nothing — alongside the claim that consonants are constantly substituted for one another. The saying was in circulation as an unattributed jest by 1833; Voltaire’s name was attached later.

source.heading: The source
source.excerpt: …où la voyelle ne fait rien, et la consonne fort peu de chose.
trail: Court de Gébelin’s Monde primitif (1775) sets out etymological principles including that vowels count for nothing in comparing words, and that corresponding consonants substitute freely — the substance of the joke, stated seriously Quote Investigator ↗.

By October 1833 the Quarterly Review was quoting it in French as a circulating saying with no author attached. The earliest English attribution to Voltaire that researchers have found is the Foreign Quarterly Review of October 1836, calling it his ‘jest’ — nearly sixty years after his death the chain ↗.

An earlier Voltaire attribution is reported in A. W. von Schlegel’s 1815 review of the Grimms’ work. We flag this as reported but unverified — it rests on a secondary listing and we have not inspected the 1815 review itself, so we do not assert it as the earliest Wikiquote ↗.
source.excerptNote: The French form as it appeared in 1833 — already a stock jest, already without an author. The Voltaire label arrives afterwards.

source.rightsNote: Free to reuse. There is no Voltaire text here, but every candidate source is long out of copyright: Court de Gébelin died in 1784, Schlegel in 1845, and the 1833 and 1836 review wordings are nineteenth-century periodical text. You may quote the French and English forms freely — just do not credit them to Voltaire. This is not legal advice.

author.name: Voltaire
author.heading: Why it gets pinned on Voltaire
author.bio: Voltaire is the default author for any French-sounding piece of learned mockery, and a jest deflating a pretentious new science is exactly his register. He also had the advantage of being dead: the saying was circulating anonymously by the 1830s, and attaching it to the most quotable Frenchman of the previous century gave it a pedigree it never had.

misattribution.heading: The attribution problem
misattribution.intro: This is a joke about a real intellectual fashion — eighteenth-century etymologists who derived any word from any other by waving away the vowels. It has a plausible origin, and Voltaire is not it.

items.why: No researcher has located it in Voltaire’s writings, and the earliest attributions to him postdate his death by decades — 1836 in English on the firmest evidence the chain ↗.

His Monde primitif lays out, as serious method, that vowels count for nothing and consonants interchange. The famous line is that method restated as ridicule — the joke is at his expense, not Voltaire’s invention.

Schlegel is said to have credited Voltaire in an 1815 review. We have not inspected that review and do not assert it — if correct it would move the earliest Voltaire attribution back two decades, still long after his death.

misattribution.truthLine: Not Voltaire. The idea belongs to Court de Gébelin’s 1775 etymological method; the saying circulated anonymously by 1833 and only later acquired his name full trail ↗.

context.heading: Why it resonates
lead: It skewers a genuine scandal of early philology: if you may discard the vowels and swap the consonants at will, you can derive any word from any other, and many eighteenth-century etymologists cheerfully did.
The joke survived because the temptation did. It still gets quoted at anyone deriving grand conclusions from surface resemblance between words — which is the same argument, two centuries later.
detailsBody: Court de Gébelin, Monde primitif (1775): vowels count for nothing; consonants substitute freely — stated as method.
Louis de Bonald (1800) and an 1807 English translation: ‘Vowels are nothing in etymology.’
Quarterly Review, October 1833: the French jest, quoted with no author.
Foreign Quarterly Review, October 1836: ‘in etymology vowels are nothing, and consonants next to nothing’ — credited to Voltaire.
context.pull: The joke is at the etymologists' expense. Voltaire just got the credit.
